Yes—**you have a reasonable chance of spotting it**, though it may take deliberate searching.

- The Moon is a **thin crescent (11.4% illuminated)**, so it is much fainter than a half or full Moon.
- At **18° altitude**, it is high enough to avoid the worst horizon haze, but still not especially high.
- It is **39° from the Sun**, with the Sun at altitude 34°. That places the Moon well away from the Sun’s immediate glare, though the daytime sky remains very bright.
- A crescent this thin can still be visible to unaided eyes in a clear sky, especially when it is this far from the Sun and reasonably high.
- The Moon’s angular size at that distance is normal, so distance does not make it unusually difficult.

Look toward **azimuth 201°**—roughly **south-southwest**—at an elevation of about **18°**, well to the right/west of the Sun’s direction (azimuth 160°). Blocking the Sun from your eyes with a building, wall, or hand will help substantially. Binoculars can locate it, but do **not** scan near the Sun with binoculars unless you are certain the Sun cannot enter the field of view.

Overall: **likely visible under genuinely clear conditions, perhaps moderately difficult rather than impossible**. If the stated sky brightness is very strong, thin haze or low contrast could still make it hard to detect.
